https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c20d.text: Figure caption, Watch: Moment powerful earthquake shakes Colombia and crumbles buildings By Michael Sheils McNamee Published 6 hours ago Rescue workers in Colombia are working against the clock to free survivors trapped in buildings and under rubble following Monday's powerful earthquake. More than 180 people have been confirmed dead - most in the cities of Cali and Pereira. The magnitude 7.4 quake struck at 07:34 (12:34 GMT) on Monday and was felt across an enormous area, stretching for hundreds of miles across western Colombia - with fresh aftershocks still being felt on Tuesday. While the official death toll remains 181, an aggregated figure gathered from local officials puts it higher - potentially at more than 240. A state of emergency has been declared by President Abelardo de la Espriella. Giving an update on Tuesday from Pereira, one of the worst hit cities, President Espriella said as well as those killed, almost 2,600 had been injured, and almost 200 people remain missing. He also reported that more than 1,100 homes had been destroyed, and more than 8,000 had been damaged. Overnight on Monday into Tuesday, several people several people spent the night outdoors in cities like Pereira and Cali - either due to their homes being destroyed, or fear of further collapses. Across the country, dozens of larger buildings have also collapsed. In Cali, a city of 2.2 million people where there have been 95 deaths, a unified command post has been set up to co-ordinate the rescue effort. On Tuesday, Cali Mayor Alejandro Eder said that 239 people remained trapped, with 949 injured and 45 buildings which have either completely or partially collapsed. Several of the upper floors of one of the city's hospitals, some dedicated to paediatric care, collapsed, leaving some patients trapped. In Calima, a neighbourhood in the north of Cali, four children died after a section of the Gimnasio Calima school collapsed. The mayor of the municipality, Antonio Cadavid, stated that other children ended up with serious injuries, with a total of 30 children were referred to care centres. To combat threats of looting, he has also ordered a curfew, coming into effect at 20:00 local time, and lasting until 06:00 on Wednesday morning. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Firefighters in Cali have worked to pulled survivors free from rubble Image source, Reuters Image caption, Rescuers searched for survivors at the site of a collapsed building in Cali Further tremors were felt in Cali on Tuesday - part of a pattern of aftershocks across the country, with more than 70 having taken place since Monday's earthquake, according to Colombia's geological service. According to the agency, two earthquakes of magnitude 3.6 occurred early on Tuesday. The first was in San JosÃ© del Palmar and the second in Santander. In Pereira, 79 people have died according to the city's fire department. The city has implemented a car-free day to allow the search to go ahead, with citizens urged to comply. Footage from the city has shown the massive scale of the rescue effort, with hundreds of volunteers working to remove rubble and free trapped survivors. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Large numbers of volunteers joined the effort to free survivors in Pereira Hours after the earthquake hit Pereira, a resident of the Parque Industrial neighborhood, near the city's airport, told BBC Mundo about the shock being experienced in the area. "It's impossible to get around the city center. In BolÃ­var Square (the city's main square), at least one building collapsed. Furthermore, there are structures where buses and trucks are trapped, and people are afraid those structures will collapse as well," he said. "We're all in shock. It was really awful." Jorge Eduardo Rojas, mayor of Manizales, said five people had been killed in the city. Sixty buildings in Manizales had partially or totally collapsed. Cautioning about further aftershocks, Rojas urged the public not to share chain messages or social media posts from unknown sources, as they "may contain false or unverified information... which could cause greater concern and alarm among the public". On Tuesday, help and support continued to be offered to Colombia from the international community. A statement from a spokesperson for UN Secretary-General, AntÃ³nio Guterres, stated that he "expresses his solidarity with the people and government of Colombia" and that it working to support the government's response. Spain's Foreign Minister, JosÃ© Manuel Albares, reported that 164 Spaniards were still missing. At the moment, he added, there are no reports of injuries or deaths of its citizens. The Donald Trump administration, which backed President Abelardo de la Espriella in his successful election earlier this year, announced this afternoon a donation of $15.5m (Â£11.5m) to Colombia. Offers of help have also come from Ecuador, Brazil, El Salvador, and Venezuela. https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/athletics/ar.text: Figure caption, Men's half marathon record broken by 29 seconds By Craig Nelson BBC Sport Journalist Published 4 hours ago Ethiopia's Yomif Kejelcha has broken the men's half marathon world record, winning a World Athletics road race in Buenos Aires on Sunday in 56 minutes 51 seconds. The 29-year-old previously held the record with a time of 57:30, set in Valencia in October 2024, but lost that to Uganda's Jacob Kiplimo in March . Kiplimo ran 57:20 in Lisbon earlier this year but Kejelcha has now knocked 29 seconds off that time to regain the record, subject to official ratification. The world track silver medallist in the 10,000m also holds the world record for a men's 10,000m road race. He also became one of the first men to run a sub-two hour marathon in record-eligible conditions earlier this year when finishing second behind Kenya's Sebastian Sawe in the London Marathon. Sawe won the record-breaking race in 1:59:30 , beating Kejelcha by just 11 seconds. https://www.politico.eu/article/kemi-bad.text: BIRMINGHAM, England — Britain’s Conservatives don’t get many opportunities to feel upbeat these days — but Kemi Badenoch is heading into party conference with a modest spring in her step. The Tory leader — who in 2024 took over an outfit near-obliterated by its worst general election result in history — can point to disarray in her chief rival’s ranks, decent personal ratings and some clear dividing lines with Labour as just a few reasons to be cheerful. Yet it’s still a massive road back for the once-dominant center-right party. Let POLITICO give you the view from Tory land as the West Midlands gathering gets going in earnest. Advertisement Advertisement On the upside 1) Badenoch’s personal ratings are on the up The British public’s view of the Tory leader has improved sharply since she took over. YouGov polling last month found 32% of voters now have a favorable view of Badenoch, compared to 47% who view her unfavorably. It’s hardly stirring stuff, but that net rating — of minus 15 — is 20 points higher than a year ago. And that is beginning to vindicate some party strategists’ belief that the more the public sees of Badenoch, the more it likes her. Robert Jenrick delivers his keynote speech during the Reform UK party conference in Birmingham, England on Sept. 5, 2026. | Dan Kitwood/Getty Images Badenoch also has no serious internal competitor trying to remove her, following Robert Jenrick’s defection to right-wing populist Reform UK earlier this year. Jenrick narrowly lost the Tory leadership race to Badenoch in 2024, and was widely seen as hankering for her job before his abrupt departure to Nigel Farage’s army. “Compared to last year when lots of people were sharpening their knives to bring Kemi down, going into this conference the mood is actually very good,” said one Tory adviser, granted anonymity to speak candidly. “Kemi has found her voice and is doing well in taking the fight to Labour.” 2) Farage has had a messy summer The party’s year has also been helped by the trials and tribulations of their chief opponents. Advertisement Advertisement The Conservatives’ main competitors on the right, Reform UK, enjoyed stellar results at May’s local elections, and there was serious talk of them eclipsing the Tories as the U.K.’s real opposition. Since then, however, Farage has faced months of scrutiny about his party’s finances, and spent the summer campaigning in a self-imposed by-election entirely focused on his own position. “A year ago, it felt like Reform UK had cannibalized the British right behind them, whereas now that seems much more up for grabs,” says Keiran Pedley, the U.K. director of politics at polling company Ipsos. “It doesn’t mean that the Tories have won that argument, but at least there is an argument to be had.” Nigel Farage speaks during a Reform UK rally in Doncaster, England on Oct. 1, 2026. | Christopher Furlong/Getty Images Reform UK still leads the Tories in national voting intention, according to POLITICO’s Poll of Polls , and it has gained a real toehold in local government that will help it build out an election-fighting machine. But, says Pedley: “If you’re a voter on the right of politics in Britain, maybe as you become less impressed by Nigel Farage, you’re also looking to Kemi Badenoch, hoping that she can be the answer.” Farage was widely criticized for failing to declare a £5 million gift he received from crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne in the 12 months before he became an MP, while there’s been a fresh flood of cash to Reform UK in recent months. Advertisement Advertisement In an eve-of-conference interview with the Tory-supporting Spectator magazine , Badenoch claimed the megabucks donations have “encouraged quite a few people to give us a bit more” to stay on the field. 3) She’s stamped her authority on the Tory top team Badenoch revamped her Shadow Cabinet at the tail-end of the summer recess in a bid to take the fight to Labour under new Prime Minister Andy Burnham. Mel Stride, who fought the 2024 leadership contest and was a staunch loyalist to ex-PM Rishi Sunak, was replaced as shadow chancellor by Andrew Griffith. Griffith spent decades in business before working for Boris Johnson, and though Labour has leapt on his time as Treasury minister during former Prime Minister Liz Truss’ budget meltdown, the Tories believe his private sector experience adds real heft. Tom Tugendhat speaks during an event in New York on Sept. 22, 2026. | Paul Morigi/Getty Images for Concordia Summit Priti Patel — a Boris Johnson-era Cabinet big-hitter — was moved out of her role as shadow foreign secretary, in favor of the well-respected Tom Tugendhat, an ex-security minister who also chaired the Commons’ Foreign Affairs Committee. Though a more centrist, one-nation Conservative, he has accepted Badenoch’s more hardline policies, like pushing to leave the European Convention on Human Rights. “At our conference, we will show the country that the Conservative Party is different from the one that lost the last election,” a Tory spokesperson said. “We will set out our plan to reverse Labour’s economic decline, build a stronger economy and a stronger country, and get Britain working again.” Advertisement Advertisement 4) Andy Burnham has opened up space for a grey vote challenge The biggest announcement from Burnham’s first conference speech as Labour leader has the potential to be a gift to the Tories, who have long felt able to rely on support from Britain’s older voters. Burnham has vowed to reform the “triple lock” — introduced by the Tories when they were last in office and all but guaranteeing generous annual state pension rises — a move that opens up space for the Conservatives to go on the attack. Privately, plenty of Tories would love to make the same move, because of the strain the triple lock places on the country’s public finances. “Literally no MP or party official think keeping the triple lock is a good thing,” the same adviser quoted above said. “It just boxes the party and the leadership in.” Andy Burnham is seen during the Labour Conference in Liverpool, England on Sept. 30, 2026. | Christopher Furlong/Getty Images But that hasn’t stopped Badenoch and her team from going straight on the attack. “His proposal to change the triple lock is already falling apart under scrutiny, and it won’t generate enough savings to fund a nationalized care system for another two decades, which means more tax rises are inevitable,” she said of Burnham last week. On the downside 1) The Tories haven’t broken through in national polls Despite Badenoch’s improved personal position, the Conservatives still lag in national polls and don’t appear anywhere close to forming a House of Commons majority after the next election. POLITICO’s Poll of Polls has seen the party slip into third place behind Labour and Reform UK ever since Keir Starmer’s resignation as PM. Hovering around the 18% to 19% mark, they’re still polling lower than the national 23.7% vote share Rishi Sunak sank to in 2024. Advertisement Advertisement Pedley warns there’s a difference between voters liking Badenoch as leader and believing the Tories have “the right plans, the right team of leaders [and are] ready to govern the country credibly in the future.” 2) A divided right could give Labour a hand Even with Reform UK’s bumpy summer, Farage’s party is a national contender — and splitting the right-wing vote in some constituencies could let Labour or the Lib Dems cruise through the middle. So far, the Conservatives and Reform UK have both insisted there will be no electoral alliance between the pair. The Tories argue it’s impossible to work with Reform UK thanks to Farage’s history of falling out with once-close allies , while Reform UK sees the Tories as damaged goods who’ve wrecked the country. (That hasn’t stopped them grabbing a fair few defectors, of course.) 3) The specter of Brexit returns Burnham also made closer relations with the European Union a key part of his conference pitch — thrusting a largely dormant part of British political discourse back to the centre. Demonstrators attend a Rejoin rally in London on June 20, 2026. | Brook Mitchell/Getty Images And it’s a divisive one for the Tories, who have spent decades riven by splits about the EU. While many former supporters of staying in the bloc have now left the Conservatives, the increased salience of Europe could reopen old wounds. Polling shows many voters believe Brexit — which the Tories presided over — hasn’t gone well. That’s not the same as wanting to rejoin altogether, but the Conservatives may now be forced to defend a project they’d just about moved on from. Advertisement

The Eastern Flank Working in Romania New Names on the Cover The Cooking Show Expat in Romania RRI Special The Sounds of Romania Voices from the Archives Our Shows Listeners’ Corner Romanian without Tears Sunday Show In the Spotlight Through the Looking Glass Change Makers Happening in Romania Music Time Artscape Weekend Edition On demand LISTEN HERE Useful information Things to know How to listen Forum QSL QSL-cards Homepage » Actualitate » The Week in Review » The Week in Review 21-25.09.2026 The Week in Review 21-25.09.2026 The headline-grabbing events of the past week in Romania The Week in Review Roxana Vasile , 26.09.2026, 14:00 Talks on forming a new government take place in Bucharest The Romanian Prime Minister designate, the Liberal Siegfried Mureșan, has this week outlined the main points of his governing program, which he intends to present before Parliament when seeking a vote of investiture. He announced plans to continue managing public funds prudently, noting that the country is set to enter a “growth phase” following the current difficult period. Among other things, he does not plan to raise fees or taxes, which have nearly tripled this year, and intends to consider public sector wage increases and pension indexation in the 2027 budget, given that Romanians’ incomes have been frozen for quite some time due to austerity measures aimed at reducing the country’s deficit. Following meetings with the PNL, USR, and UDMR, Siegfried Mureșan announced that he has the political backing of the three parties currently forming the interim government in Bucharest. However, together they hold only 170 parliamentary seats, whereas a minimum of 233 is required to confirm his government. Nevertheless, the Prime Minister designate remains confident that he can also hold talks with the PSD in an effort to persuade them to vote for him. In response, the Social Democrats have called on Mureșan to step down, asserting that he has no chance of securing a parliamentary majority vote. Previously, the PSD had also called on him to resign his position of MEP to demonstrate that he genuinely intends to become Prime Minister. AUR (the nationalist opposition), excluded from the negotiations, reiterated that it would not vote for a government of which it is not a part. If Siegfried Mureșan fails to secure parliamentary approval, Romania could face the prospect of early elections, a scenario that the country’s president, Nicușor Dan, wishes to avoid. In his view, such elections would prolong the uncertainty that has prevailed since May, when the current government was dismissed via a no-confidence motion. In New York President Dan attended the UN General Assembly Support for Ukraine and Russia’s hybrid threats were among the topics addressed by President Nicușor Dan during his national address at the United Nations. On Wednesday in New York, speaking from the UN General Assembly podium, the Romanian President drew attention to manipulation via social media, a threat to democracies. The head of state explained that the fundamental principle of democracy is “one person, one voice, one vote”, and if thousands of fake accounts express themselves in a coordinated manner, the individual’s voice is no longer heard, and freedom of expression is denied. Addressing the war in Ukraine, Nicușor Dan once again reiterated his support for the Ukrainian people for as long as necessary. He warned that the Russian Federation’s hybrid threats are not directed solely at Ukraine but target all of Europe. In the Romanian President’s view, these threats can only be deterred by increasing military spending. Black Sea security, support for the Republic of Moldova, the peace plan for Gaza, and Romania’s openness to business and innovation were among the other topics Nicușor Dan covered in his national address at the UN. While in the United States, the President also met with members of the Romanian community in New York and inaugurated the “Queen Marie of Romania Intersection” to mark the centenary of the Romanian sovereign’s historic tour of the U.S. On the occasion, an anniversary plaque was unveiled at the intersection of 38 th Street and 3 rd Avenue, near the headquarters of Romania’s Permanent Mission to the UN. S&P experts assess Romania’s sovereign rating Experts from the international agency Standard & Poor’s have arrived in Bucharest this week to assess Romania’s economic and fiscal developments with a view to determining its sovereign rating. In a social media post, the interim Finance Minister Alexandru Nazare stated that his ministry’s primary objective during this period is to maintain the rating; this rating determines the terms under which Romania borrows from foreign markets and influences investor confidence, as well as the availability of funds for development rather than interest payments. Standard & Poor’s, one of the world’s leading rating agencies, is to publish its periodic report on Romania on October 2. The current rating is at the lower end of the “investment-grade” category. A downgrade would push the country into “junk” status, that is not recommended for investment. Romanians’ Economic Sentiment Meanwhile, the benchmarks used to calculate the cost of variable-rate consumer and mortgage loans in the national currency have risen. Pump prices for petrol and diesel have surpassed new psychological thresholds. The leu has depreciated significantly against major currencies, hitting an all-time high against the euro. And although the pace of inflation slowed, dropping to 6.17% in August from 8.16% in July, the cost of services continued to rise at a double-digit rate, driven by hikes in energy and fuel prices. Prices for foods and non-foods have also risen, with dramatic consequences for low-income households. Consequently, nearly a third of Romanians (32%) say they are worse off than a year ago, with the disparity clearly visible between their earnings and their purchasing power. People remain pessimistic about the economy, and 86% expect further price increases; as a result, they are more cautious and are attempting to adjust their behavior to an economic environment perceived as difficult and enduring, according to a study by INSCOP released this week. https://www.politico.eu/article/andy-bur.text: LONDON — Andy Burnham offered his “rock-solid” support to Ukraine as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy prepares to visit the U.K. Wednesday. The British prime minister urged international allies to strengthen sanctions on Russia and called on President Vladimir Putin to agree to an energy ceasefire ahead of Zelenskyy's visit to Downing Street. It will be the first visit to a European capital by the Ukrainian president since Donald Trump temporarily lifted sanctions on Russian diesel last Friday. In a statement issued by No. 10 ahead of the visit, Burnham said: “Our rock-solid support to Ukraine is vital for keeping us safe here in the UK and ensuring those on the frontlines have the equipment they need to push back Russia. Advertisement Advertisement “My message to the Ukrainian people could not be clearer, we are with you for as long as it takes, and we will go further and faster in our support to back your courageous fight for peace in Europe. It is not just the right thing to do, but it's the necessary thing to do. Russia's aggression cannot be allowed to succeed on our continent.” Downing Street said the U.K. prime minister has asked ministers to draw up proposals for further sanctions, military aid, and fiscal packages to support Ukraine in the coming weeks. Britain will deliver £45 million of surface-to-air missiles and implement a ban on Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports. Britain will also accelerate deliveries of more than 5,000 Lightweight Multirole Missiles to Ukraine over the next four years with £1.6 billion funding, Downing Street added. Chancellor John Healey will use meetings at the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in Bangkok to urge other countries to impose an equivalent LNG ban, arguing it would “curtail the war chest funding Putin so desperately wants.” European leaders are expected to use a European Council summit Thursday to back stronger sanctions on Moscow after Trump struck a deal with Russia to ease restrictions on its diesel exports. https://www.bursa.ro/young-romanians-eur.text: Young people in Romania live in households where the equivalized disposable income is only 33.7% of the European Union average, according to 2025 Eurostat data recently presented by Euronews. Meanwhile, regarding personal wage earnings, Romanian employees under the age of 30 reached approximately half of the EU average in 2022-specifically, 50.6%. Although these are two distinct metrics covering different years and age groups, both highlight the significant financial gap that remains relative to the European benchmark. In an analysis published on October 26, Euronews reports that the median annual equivalized disposable income for young people aged 18-24 is 7,237 euros in Romania, compared to 21,482 euros in the EU. This calculation begins with household income after taxes and adjusts it based on the number and ages of the household members. In other words, it measures the household resources allocated to each individual, rather than the personal earnings of a young person. Romania lags behind several other member states in the region: Hungary records 8,576 euros, Bulgaria 8,680 euros, and Croatia 15,921 euros. In the latter case, the figure is more than double the level seen in Romania. If we shift our focus from household budgets to income earned through employment, a different picture emerges. The study "Wage Disparities: Influencing Factors in 2022," published by the National Institute of Statistics (INS) in 2024, shows that employees in Romania aged 15-24 had an average annual gross wage of 49,238 lei. The average for all employees included in the research was 77,416 lei. Consequently, young people earned approximately 36.4% less. Based on the 2022 average exchange rate from the National Bank of Romania (BNR), the figure for the 15-24 age group amounts to approximately 9,984 euros in annual gross earnings. This represents individual earnings-before taxes-for employees working in enterprises with at least ten staff members. It does not reflect the income of all young Romanians; those without a wage are not included in this average. In Eurostat data for 2022, the youngest age category reported is "under 30 years old." For Romania, the average annual gross wage was 14,724 euros, compared to 29,099 euros for the EU as a whole. Romania ranked 23rd out of the 27 member states. The research covers enterprises with at least ten employees and excludes the agriculture and public administration sectors. In this comparison, Romania ranked ahead of Poland (14,435 euros), Hungary (14,411 euros), Croatia (14,013 euros), and Bulgaria (12,496 euros). However, it ranked below Slovakia (euro16,600), the Czech Republic (euro18,901), and Slovenia (euro24,430). The contrast is stark: in a recent comparison of the resources of households where young people reside, Romania ranks below Bulgaria, Hungary, and Croatia-yet it ranks above them in 2022 statistics regarding the gross wages of employees under the age of 30. We cannot interpret this discrepancy as a narrative of progress or decline, given the variations in the years, age groups, populations analyzed, and specific indicators used across the statistics published to date on this subject by the National Institute of Statistics (INS) and Eurostat. Nevertheless, it is fair to say that a wage-based ranking captures only one aspect of a generation's financial situation. Similarly, the gap between the approximately euro9,984 figure derived from INS data and the euro14,724 figure from Eurostat cannot be interpreted as a salary increase. The latter figure includes employees aged 25-29, and the scope of economic activities covered also differs. Beyond these distinctions lies the issue of independence. In an analysis by Euronews, the European Youth Forum warns that living with one's parents can artificially improve the statistical profile of young people-even when, in reality, they cannot afford to move out. For Romania, the uncomfortable question begins here: what can a young person actually build using their own income, once housing costs and daily living expenses are covered? While a job and a shared household budget with one's parents may sustain one's current standard of living, they do not necessarily provide a path toward true independence. The ability to rent a place of one's own, to save money, and to make plans without family support reveals just how much financial freedom that income actually provides.
